Faraday's law applies to any change in flux, here caused by the changing current in a nearby circuit; Lenz's law gives the sense.

A current is induced in the second loop as long as the first loop carries a steady current, because the second loop is in the magnetic field of the first. is incorrect: Believes that the presence of a magnetic field, not its change, induces an emf.
No current is induced in the second loop, because the two loops are not connected by a wire. is incorrect: Believes that induction requires a conducting connection between circuits.

payload.title: Two batteries and three resistors: Kirchhoff's rules

stimulus.description: Two batteries of emfs $\varepsilon_1=12\text{ V}$ and $\varepsilon_2=12\text{ V}$ with negligible internal resistance have their positive terminals connected to the same wire (the top wire) and their negative terminals connected to the bottom wire. Battery 1 is in series with $R_1=6\,\Omega$ and battery 2 is in series with $R_2=4\,\Omega$ in separate branches, and a resistor $R_3=3\,\Omega$ connects the top wire to the bottom wire.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw a schematic diagram of the circuit and label the three branch currents $I_1$ (through battery 1), $I_2$ (through battery 2) and $I_3$ (through $R_3$) with arrows showing the directions in which they flow.
parts.model_answer: Three branches in parallel between the top and bottom wires; $I_1$ and $I_2$ leave the positive terminals toward the top wire and $I_3$ flows from the top wire through $R_3$ to the bottom wire.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws three parallel branches (battery 1 with $R_1$, battery 2 with $R_2$, and $R_3$) joined at a top and a bottom wire
common_errors: draws all elements in series

rubric_rows.criterion: Marks the polarity of both batteries with the positive terminals on the top wire
common_errors: reverses the polarity of one battery

rubric_rows.criterion: Labels $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$ with arrows toward the top wire for $I_1$ and $I_2$ and downward through $R_3$ for $I_3$
common_errors: draws $I_3$ upward through $R_3$

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Use Kirchhoff's rules to derive an expression for the current $I_3$ in $R_3$ in terms of $\varepsilon_1$, $\varepsilon_2$, $R_1$, $R_2$ and $R_3$.
parts.model_answer: The junction rule gives $I_3=I_1+I_2$ and the loop rules give $\varepsilon_1-I_1R_1-I_3R_3=0$ and $\varepsilon_2-I_2R_2-I_3R_3=0$; eliminating $I_1$ and $I_2$ gives $I_3=\dfrac{\varepsilon_1R_2+\varepsilon_2R_1}{R_1R_2+R_1R_3+R_2R_3}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the junction rule $I_3=I_1+I_2$
common_errors: writes $I_3=I_1-I_2$ for the stated directions

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes a correct loop equation for each battery loop, for example $\varepsilon_1-I_1R_1-I_3R_3=0$ and $\varepsilon_2-I_2R_2-I_3R_3=0$
common_errors: omits the voltage drop across $R_3$ in one loop

rubric_rows.criterion: Eliminates $I_1$ and $I_2$ to obtain $I_3=(\varepsilon_1R_2+\varepsilon_2R_1)/(R_1R_2+R_1R_3+R_2R_3)$
common_errors: algebra error in the elimination

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the current in $R_3$ and the power dissipated in $R_3$ for the given values.
parts.model_answer: $I_3\approx2.22\text{ A}$ and $P_3=I_3^2R_3\approx14.8\text{ W}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $I_3$ of about 2.22 with units of amperes (accept any value within 2 percent)
common_errors: uses $\varepsilon_1/(R_1+R_3)$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the power $P_3=I_3^2R_3$ of about 14.8 with units of watts

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Both emfs are doubled while all the resistances stay the same. By what factor does the power dissipated in $R_3$ change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The power increases by a factor of 4: every current in the linear circuit is proportional to the emfs, so $I_3$ doubles and $P_3=I_3^2R_3$ becomes four times $14.8\text{ W}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the power increases by a factor of 4
common_errors: states that the power doubles
states that the power is unchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that all currents are proportional to the emfs (a linear circuit) so $I_3$ doubles, and that $P=I^2R$ depends on the square of the current
common_errors: argues only that more voltage means more power

payload.title: Magnetic field inside a wire with a nonuniform current density

stimulus.description: A long straight cylindrical wire of radius $R=2\text{ mm}$ carries a current along its axis. The current density depends on the distance $r$ from the axis as $J(r)=J_0r/R$, where $J_0=2\times10^{5}\text{ A/m}^{2}$. Use $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the diagram of the cross-section of the wire (shown as a circle, with the current out of the page), draw a circular Amperian loop of radius $r<R$ and draw an arrow showing the direction of the magnetic field on the loop.
parts.model_answer: A circle concentric with the wire inside its boundary, with the field arrow tangent to the circle and pointing counterclockwise for a current out of the page.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a circular loop concentric with the wire and inside its boundary ($r<R$)
required_elements: concentric loop of radius r < R
common_errors: draws the loop off-center or outside the wire

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws the field arrow tangent to the loop (perpendicular to the radius)
common_errors: draws a radial arrow

rubric_rows.criterion: Gives the correct sense, counterclockwise for a current out of the page, by the right-hand rule
common_errors: draws a clockwise arrow

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance $r<R$ from the axis in terms of $\mu_0$, $J_0$, $R$ and $r$.
parts.model_answer: $I_{enc}=\int_0^rJ_0\dfrac{r'}{R}2\pi r'\,dr'=\dfrac{2\pi J_0r^3}{3R}$ and Ampère's law $B\,2\pi r=\mu_0I_{enc}$ gives $B=\dfrac{\mu_0J_0r^2}{3R}$.

payload.title: Induced emf from a changing field: graph, Faraday's law and prediction

stimulus.description: A square loop of side $20\text{ cm}$ and total resistance $0.5\,\Omega$ lies in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its plane. The magnitude of the field changes with time as follows: it increases linearly from $0$ to $B_1=0.5\text{ T}$ between $t=0$ and $t=2\text{ s}$, stays constant between $t=2\text{ s}$ and $t=4\text{ s}$, and decreases linearly back to $0$ between $t=4\text{ s}$ and $t=6\text{ s}$. Blank axes are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the induced emf $\varepsilon$ in the loop as a function of time from $t=0$ to $t=6\text{ s}$, taking the emf during the first interval as positive. Label the value of the emf in the first interval in terms of the quantities given.
parts.model_answer: A positive constant $\varepsilon=AB_1/(2\text{ s})$ from $0$ to $2$ s, zero from $2$ s to $4$ s, and an equal-magnitude negative constant from $4$ s to $6$ s (three flat segments with steps at $2$ s and $4$ s).

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units
The emf is constant and positive from $0$ to $2$ s with the labeled value $AB_1/(2\text{ s})$
common_errors: draws a ramp instead of a constant emf

rubric_rows.criterion: The emf is zero from $2$ s to $4$ s
required_elements: zero emf in the middle interval
common_errors: draws the emf equal to the field in the middle interval

rubric_rows.criterion: The emf is negative with the same magnitude from $4$ s to $6$ s
required_elements: equal and opposite emf in the last interval
common_errors: draws a positive emf for the decreasing field

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Use Faraday's law to derive an expression for the magnitude of the emf in the first interval in terms of $s$ (the side length), $B_1$ and the duration $T$ of the interval.
parts.model_answer: $\Phi=s^2B(t)$ and $B=B_1t/T$, so $|\varepsilon|=d\Phi/dt=s^2B_1/T$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the flux through the loop $\Phi=s^2B(t)$ (the field is perpendicular to the plane)
common_errors: uses a different area

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the field as $B(t)=B_1t/T$ and differentiates
common_errors: differentiates the area instead of the field

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $|\varepsilon|=s^2B_1/T$
common_errors: omits the area

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the emf in the first interval and the total charge that flows through the loop during that interval.
parts.model_answer: $|\varepsilon|=s^2B_1/T\approx10.00\text{ mV}$ and $q=\varepsilon T/R=\Delta\Phi/R\approx40.00\text{ mC}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the emf of about 10.00 with units of millivolts (accept any value within 2 percent)
common_errors: leaves the side in centimeters

rubric_rows.criterion: Relates the current to the emf, $I=\varepsilon/R$, and the charge to the current, $q=IT$ (or $q=\Delta\Phi/R$)
common_errors: uses $q=\varepsilon R$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the charge of about 40.00 with units of millicoulombs

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The loop is rotated about an axis in its plane so that its normal makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the field, and the field changes in the same way. By what factor does the emf in the first interval change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The flux is $s^2B\cos60^\circ$, so the emf is multiplied by $\cos60^\circ=0.5$ (from $10.00\text{ mV}$ to $5.00\text{ mV}$).

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the emf is multiplied by 0.5 (it is halved)
common_errors: states that the emf is unchanged
states a factor of $\sin60^\circ$

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$: only the component of the field along the normal contributes to the flux
common_errors: argues only that tilting the loop changes the area

payload.title: Discharge of a capacitor: graph, derivation and energy

stimulus.description: A capacitor of capacitance $C=10\,\mu\text{F}$ is charged to a potential difference $V_0=9\text{ V}$ and then, at $t=0$, connected across a resistor of resistance $R=10\text{ k}\Omega$. Blank axes are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the potential difference $V$ across the capacitor as a function of time from $t=0$ to about five time constants. Label the initial value and mark the time constant and the value of $V$ at that time.
parts.model_answer: A decaying exponential that starts at $V_0=9\text{ V}$, has its steepest slope at $t=0$ and approaches zero, passing through about $3.31\text{ V}$ (37 percent of $V_0$) at $t=\tau=RC=100\text{ ms}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units
The curve starts at the labeled value $V_0=9\text{ V}$ at $t=0$
common_errors: starts at zero

rubric_rows.criterion: The curve decays exponentially toward zero with a decreasing slope and never goes negative
common_errors: draws a straight line to zero

rubric_rows.criterion: Marks $t=\tau=RC$ and the value about $0.37V_0$ there
common_errors: marks the point where the voltage is half of $V_0$ as $\tau$

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Use Kirchhoff's loop rule to derive an expression for $V(t)$ in terms of $V_0$, $R$, $C$ and $t$.
parts.model_answer: $V=IR$ with $I=-dq/dt$ and $q=CV$ gives $V=-RC\,dV/dt$; separating variables and integrating with $V(0)=V_0$ gives $V=V_0e^{-t/RC}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the loop equation $q/C-IR=0$ with $I=-dq/dt$ (or $V=-RC\,dV/dt$)
common_errors: omits the minus sign for the decreasing charge

rubric_rows.criterion: Separates variables and integrates with $V(0)=V_0$
common_errors: uses $V(0)=0$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $V(t)=V_0e^{-t/RC}$
common_errors: obtains $1-e^{-t/RC}$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the time at which the energy stored in the capacitor has fallen to half of its initial value.
parts.model_answer: The energy is $\tfrac12CV^2$, so it is half of the initial value when $V=V_0/\sqrt2$: $t=\tfrac12RC\ln2\approx34.66\text{ ms}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Notes that the energy $U=\tfrac12CV^2$ is proportional to $V^2$, so $V=V_0/\sqrt2$ when $U=U_0/2$
common_errors: sets $V=V_0/2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves $e^{-t/RC}=1/\sqrt2$ to obtain $t=\tfrac12RC\ln2$
common_errors: obtains $t=RC\ln2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 34.66 with units of milliseconds (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The capacitor is replaced by one with twice the capacitance, charged to the same initial potential difference. By what factor does the time for the voltage to fall to $V_0/e$ change? By what factor does the initial energy change? Justify your answers.
parts.model_answer: The time constant $RC$ doubles, so the time doubles; the initial energy $\tfrac12CV_0^2$ also doubles.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that both the time and the initial energy double (factor 2 for each)
common_errors: states that the time is unchanged because the voltage is the same

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $\tau=RC$ (proportional to $C$) and $U_0=\tfrac12CV_0^2$ (proportional to $C$)
common_errors: argues only that a bigger capacitor holds more charge

expected_values.quantity: time for the energy to halve

payload.title: Experiment: resistivity from resistance versus length

stimulus.description: A student measures the resistance $R$ of pieces of the same resistance wire, of diameter $d=0.5\text{ mm}$, for several lengths $L$.

notes: A student measures the resistance $R$ of pieces of the same resistance wire, of diameter $d=0.5\text{ mm}$, for several lengths $L$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the resistance as a function of the length. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the length is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the resistance.
parts.model_answer: Stretch a single wire straight along a meterstick, connect it in a circuit with a battery and an ammeter, measure the potential difference across the section of length $L$ with a voltmeter and the current with the ammeter, change the length by moving the contact, and compute $R=V/I$; keep the same wire and temperature, and reduce the uncertainty by using small currents (to limit heating) or by repeating and averaging.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies how the resistance is found (voltmeter across the section and ammeter in series, $R=V/I$, or an ohmmeter) and how the length is measured
common_errors: measures the length without a way to get the resistance

rubric_rows.criterion: Changes only the length while keeping the same wire (diameter and material) and the temperature the same
required_elements: change only the length, same wire and temperature

rubric_rows.criterion: Reduces the uncertainty by using small currents to avoid heating, or by repeating the measurement and averaging, or by using a longer range of lengths (any one earns the point)
required_elements: small currents or repeat and average or longer range (any one earns the point)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: For a uniform wire $R=\rho L/A$. Identify the quantities that should be plotted on the vertical and horizontal axes so that the data produce a straight line whose slope can be used to determine the resistivity $\rho$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies $R$ (vertical) versus $L$ (horizontal), with slope $\rho/A$

stimulus.description: A student measures the resistance $R$ of pieces of the same resistance wire, of diameter $d=0.3\text{ mm}$, for several lengths $L$.

notes: A student measures the resistance $R$ of pieces of the same resistance wire, of diameter $d=0.3\text{ mm}$, for several lengths $L$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the resistance as a function of the length. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the length is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the resistance.
parts.model_answer: Stretch a single wire straight along a meterstick, connect it in a circuit with a battery and an ammeter, measure the potential difference across the section of length $L$ with a voltmeter and the current with the ammeter, change the length by moving the contact, and compute $R=V/I$; keep the same wire and temperature, and reduce the uncertainty by using small currents (to limit heating) or by repeating and averaging.

payload.title: Field of a charged spherical shell

stimulus.description: A thin spherical shell of radius $R=10\text{ cm}$ carries a charge $Q=4\text{ nC}$ spread uniformly over its surface. The shell is nonconducting and in vacuum. Use $k=9.0\times10^{9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that the electric field at the center of the shell is the same as the electric field just outside its surface. Do you agree or disagree with the claim? Justify your answer using Gauss's law.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. For a spherical Gaussian surface inside the shell no charge is enclosed, so by symmetry and Gauss's law the field there is zero, while just outside the field is $kQ/R^2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim
common_errors: agrees because the field is continuous

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that a spherical Gaussian surface inside the shell encloses no charge, so the field inside is zero
common_errors: says the field is zero because the charges cancel pairwise without using Gauss's law

rubric_rows.criterion: Contrasts this with a surface just outside, which encloses the whole charge $Q$ and gives a nonzero field $kQ/R^2$
common_errors: says the outside field is also zero

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the electric field at a distance $r>R$ from the center and calculate its value at $r=R$ (just outside the surface).
parts.model_answer: $E\,4\pi r^2=Q/\varepsilon_0$ gives $E=kQ/r^2$; at $r=R$ it is $\approx3600\text{ N/C}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Gauss's law with a concentric spherical surface: $E\,4\pi r^2=Q/\varepsilon_0$
common_errors: uses the surface area $2\pi r^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $E=kQ/r^2$
common_errors: obtains $kQ/r$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the field at $r=R$ of about 3600 with units of newtons per coulomb (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The same shell is observed at a distance twice as far from its center, $r=2R$. Predict the factor by which the field changes compared with the value just outside the surface, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: The field falls to one quarter (about $900\text{ N/C}$), because outside the shell $E\propto1/r^2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the field is multiplied by one quarter (0.25)
common_errors: states that the field is halved
states that the field is unchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $E=kQ/r^2$ (the shell acts like a point charge at its center outside)
common_errors: argues only that the field is weaker farther away

payload.title: Energy balance while charging a capacitor

stimulus.description: A battery of emf $\varepsilon=12\text{ V}$ and negligible internal resistance charges an initially uncharged capacitor of capacitance $C=50\,\mu\text{F}$ through a resistor. The capacitor ends fully charged.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that all of the energy supplied by the battery during the charging is stored in the capacitor. Do you agree or disagree with the claim? Justify your answer by comparing the work done by the battery with the energy stored.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. The battery does work $q\varepsilon=C\varepsilon^2$ on the charge it moves, but the capacitor stores only $\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$; the other half is dissipated as thermal energy in the resistor.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim
common_errors: agrees that the energy is conserved in the capacitor

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by identifying the work done by the battery as $Q\varepsilon=C\varepsilon^2$
common_errors: uses $\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$ for the battery's work

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares with the energy stored, $\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$, and concludes that the remainder is dissipated in the resistor
common_errors: says the remainder is stored in the wires

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive expressions for the work done by the battery, the energy stored in the capacitor, and the thermal energy dissipated in the resistor, and calculate the thermal energy for the given values.
parts.model_answer: $W_{battery}=C\varepsilon^2$, $U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$ and $Q_{thermal}=W_{battery}-U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2\approx3600\,\mu\text{J}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the battery's work as $W=q\varepsilon$ with $q=C\varepsilon$, giving $C\varepsilon^2$
common_errors: writes $W=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the stored energy $U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$ and the thermal energy $Q=W-U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$
common_errors: states that the thermal energy depends on $R$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the thermal energy of about 3600 with units of microjoules (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The experiment is repeated with a resistor of twice the resistance. Predict whether the thermal energy dissipated in the resistor increases, decreases or stays the same, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: The thermal energy stays the same, because the total energy dissipated is $\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$ regardless of $R$; a larger $R$ only makes the charging slower.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the thermal energy stays the same
common_errors: states that the thermal energy doubles because $P=I^2R$

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with the energy balance: the dissipated energy equals $W-U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$, which does not depend on $R$
required_elements: Q = 1/2 C epsilon^2 independent of R
common_errors: argues only that the current is smaller with a larger resistor
